questions.stem: While trying to 'understand a problem', which of the following questions should we not bother about?
options: How do I test the solution?
questions.explanation: Understanding the problem focuses on the what: inputs, outputs and the process. Testing the solution belongs to a later stage, after the solution has been designed and implemented — there is nothing to test yet.

questions.stem: Any problem that can be solved with an arithmetic operation is known as a ___________ problem.
questions.explanation: Routine problems can be solved with an arithmetic operation. They provide a question that needs an answer plus required facts/numbers, can be solved with algorithms, and are solved quickly.

questions.stem: Any problem that does not have a standard method for solving it is known as a ___________ problem.
questions.explanation: Non-routine problems use procedures and answers that are not immediately clear. They require a distinct, unconventional thinking process based on originality and creativity, and a 'novel' method has to be developed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an attribute of routine problems?
options: Provides a question that needs an answer, in addition to some required facts or numbers
Can usually be solved using various unconventional approaches
Is solely about identifying the most appropriate algorithm to apply to the problem
questions.explanation: Routine problems are solved with standard arithmetic/algorithms — needing the most appropriate algorithm only. 'Unconventional approaches' describe NON-routine problems, which require originality and creativity.

questions.stem: Chidi is asked to provide an approximate number of hairs on his head. This is best classified as a ___________ problem.
questions.explanation: Estimating the number of hairs on your head is given in the slides as a classic NON-routine example: there is no standard method, so a novel approach (studying the problem, gathering information, implementing an effective strategy) is required.

questions.stem: Problems that can be solved with a systematic method (i.e. an algorithm) are known as ___________ problems.
questions.explanation: Any mathematical problem that can be solved with a systematic method (an algorithm) can be solved by the universal Turing machine — such problems are known as solvable problems.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of an undecidable problem?
options: Determining whether my code has a bug
Calculating the area of a 150m x 2000m parking space
Finding the sum of two numbers
Determining the maximum of a set of numbers
questions.explanation: Examples of undecidable problems are 'Does my code have a bug?' and the halting problem — no algorithm can give an accurate true/false for every input. The other options are routine, solvable problems.

questions.stem: Alan Turing introduced a 'universal computing machine' now referred to as the universal Turing machine (UTM). The modern ___________ is based on the UTM.
questions.explanation: The modern computer is based on the UTM: any task we can write an instruction table for can be implemented by the UTM, and a single machine of fixed structure can carry out every computation the UTM can carry out.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about the trial-and-error problem solving strategy?
options: It can be time consuming when the number of possible solutions to the problem are not few
It is very efficient when the number of possible solutions to the problem are not few
It involves trying various solutions until the problem is solved
It is recommended for cases where the number of possible solutions to the problem are few
questions.explanation: Trial-and-error is useful where the possible solutions are FEW, but it is time consuming and inefficient where MANY solutions exist — so claiming it is 'very efficient when solutions are not few' is the false statement (it contradicts the other true options).

questions.stem: A problem-solving strategy is a ___________ used to find a solution or overcome a challenge.
questions.explanation: A problem-solving strategy is a plan used to find a solution or overcome a challenge; it includes multiple steps that provide helpful guidelines on how to resolve a problem.

questions.stem: _________ is a group focused technique where people come together to solve a problem, involving critical thinking and coming up with various solutions spontaneously.
questions.explanation: Brainstorming is a group-focused technique: people come together, avoid criticism of ideas, and gather as many ideas as possible so the ideas of other people can be fine-tuned.

questions.stem: Tolu uses a rule of thumb to quickly choose between different brands of food items at the grocery store, accepting that his choice may not be the best one. Which strategy is Tolu using?
questions.explanation: Heuristics (rule of thumb) help obtain solutions while saving time and energy. Problems are solved fast and efficiently, but solutions are not always rational — relevant where sub-optimal solutions are acceptable.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about heuristics?
options: Problems are solved in a fast and efficient manner
They are relevant to situations where sub-optimal solutions to a problem are acceptable
They always produce the optimal solution to a problem
questions.explanation: Heuristic solutions are NOT always rational and can be sub-optimal — the claim that they 'always produce the optimal solution' is the false statement.

questions.stem: _________ analysis involves thinking about the solution beforehand, breaking a problem into smaller problems and solving them with the best possible approach until the main problem is solved.
questions.explanation: Means-ends analysis: think about the solution beforehand, determine the best strategy based on the issues to be encountered, break the problem into smaller problems, and solve them until the main problem is solved.

questions.stem: _________ is a technique of filtering out the unneeded attributes of the problem to be solved so that we can concentrate on the important parts.
questions.explanation: Abstraction removes all aspects or patterns of the problem that will not help arrive at a solution, forming an essential idea of what the problem is and how to solve it — the idea formed is also known as a model.

questions.stem: _________ deals with using previously existing understanding to understand a new similar system, as long as the underlying principles are the same.
questions.explanation: Analogy uses previously existing understanding to understand a new similar system. Steps: define the problem and generate analogies, find similarities and select an analogy, then use the description and similarities to generate ideas.

questions.stem: Which of the following algorithm design methods is used in the merge sort algorithm?
questions.explanation: Merge sort is explicitly given as a divide and conquer algorithm: the list is split into smaller easier parts, each part is solved, and the solutions are combined to sort the set of numbers.

questions.stem: _________ deals with evaluating if a program works as expected or not before it is released, and using this knowledge to make it more effective.
questions.explanation: Performance testing evaluates if a system or program works as expected before release: come up with test scenarios and success criteria, then measure performance against them (e.g. erroneous data handling, stress testing).

questions.stem: With the ___________ algorithm, a problem is solved by going through all possible choices until a solution is found.
questions.explanation: Brute force solely relies on computing power and works by trying every possibility instead of improving efficiency with advanced techniques. Brute force algorithms are simple and consistent, but very slow.

questions.stem: Aba forgot the combination to a small padlock with 4 digits (each 0-9). She decides to try every possible combination until the lock opens. Which approach is Aba using?
questions.explanation: Trying every possibility of the 4-digit lock is the slides' brute force example — it relies solely on computing power and tries all choices until a solution is found.

questions.stem: With the ___________ algorithm, the best possible solution is applied at each stage when solving a problem.
questions.explanation: The greedy algorithm always selects the best optimal path at each stage, aiming at achieving the optimal solution. It might not always produce an optimal solution, but where it does, the solutions are simple and highly efficient.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about the greedy algorithm?
options: It applies the best possible solution at each stage when solving a problem
It might not always produce an optimal solution
It guarantees that an optimal solution can be found, provided that a solution to the problem exists
Where it produces optimal solutions, those solutions are always simple and highly efficient
questions.explanation: 'Guarantees an optimal solution whenever one exists' describes DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING, not greedy. The greedy algorithm only aims at the optimal solution and might not always produce one.

questions.stem: With ___________, problems are broken into sub-problems, and the solutions of the sub-problems are saved so that there is no need to compute the result again.
questions.explanation: Dynamic programming saves sub-problem solutions for reuse. Provided a solution exists, it guarantees an optimal solution, and it is mostly used for optimization problems (min/max) such as the Fibonacci series.

questions.stem: A maze-solving algorithm traverses possible paths; at every step a decision is made about which option to follow, and at a final state it checks whether the state is accepted or rejected and then 'backtracks' to a previous state to try other unconsidered options. Which approach is this?
questions.explanation: Backtracking examines more than one possible solution; most times it uses recursion to move from one problem state to another, and 'backtracks' to a previous state to try unconsidered options — a maze is the given example.

questions.stem: _________ deals with extracting valuable information from large data sets by discovering unnoticed patterns and underlying relationships within the data.
questions.explanation: Data mining discovers underlying relationships within large data sets (big data) using techniques such as machine learning and statistical analysis, helping with informed decisions and future trend prediction.

questions.stem: A/an ___________ is a procedure of steps used to solve a given problem.
questions.explanation: Algorithms are step-by-step procedures for solving a problem and are plans for solving problems. Coding is writing the program; pseudocode and flowchart are only REPRESENTATIONS of an algorithm.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true? Algorithms can be represented as a ___________
questions.explanation: Algorithms can be represented as pseudocodes or flowcharts, and can be expressed in natural language, programming code or mathematical symbols. 'Syntax' is a set of LANGUAGE RULES, not a way to represent an algorithm.

questions.stem: _________ analysis is carried out after an algorithm has been implemented in a particular programming language, and deals with issues such as the space and running time requirements of an algorithm.
questions.explanation: Per the MIVA quiz answer key: posterior analysis is carried out AFTER implementation in a particular programming language and deals with the space and running time requirements of the algorithm.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the LAST step in the algorithm development process?
questions.explanation: The five algorithm development steps in order: 1) Problem description, 2) Problem analysis, 3) High-level algorithm development, 4) Algorithm refinement, 5) Algorithm review — so the last step is the algorithm review.

questions.stem: _________ complexity deals with the time required by an algorithm to complete its execution.
questions.explanation: Algorithm complexity is analysed in terms of time complexity (time required to complete execution) and space complexity (amount of computer space required). Best/worst/average cases are measures of TIME complexity for input size n.

questions.stem: _________ complexity deals with the amount of computer space required by an algorithm to complete its execution.
questions.explanation: Space complexity deals with the amount of computer space required by an algorithm to complete its execution. Both time and space complexity can be represented with notations such as the Big O notation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of algorithms?
options: Algorithms should have input values that will be processed to produce some output
Algorithms should have straightforward and clear instructions
Algorithms should be dependent on a particular programming language
Algorithms should have a limited and countable number of instructions
questions.explanation: Algorithms should NOT be dependent on any programming language — that is the false (NOT) statement. The other three are listed characteristics of algorithms.

questions.stem: To be easily translatable into various programming languages, algorithms should be represented in a form that has:
questions.explanation: Algorithms should be represented with all three: SEQUENCE (steps ordered one after the other), SELECTION (steps executed selectively when conditions are satisfied), and REPETITION (same steps executed repeatedly).

questions.stem: The Big O notation is very useful because it describes the ___________ of algorithms.
questions.explanation: When comparing two algorithms to know which is more efficient, the most important factor is the growth rate of both algorithms — the Big O notation describes that growth rate (e.g. constant, linear, quadratic, exponential).

questions.stem: The ___________ symbol is used in complex flowcharts to connect independent elements across multiple pages.
questions.explanation: The link or off-page connector connects independent elements across MULTIPLE pages, while the on-page connector connects elements across a SINGLE page — MIVA contrasts the two constantly.

questions.stem: A ___________ flowchart ensures that the communication gap between the users and developers of the system is reduced.
questions.explanation: Data flowcharts describe the data processing aspect of a system's design and analysis by showing the flow of information — they also ensure the communication gap between users and developers is reduced.

questions.stem: A flowchart is a ___________ representation of the sequence of operations in a computer program.
questions.explanation: A flowchart is the GRAPHICAL representation of the sequence of operations in a computer program (or of an algorithm). The TEXTUAL representation is pseudocode — the classic MIVA pair.

questions.stem: The start/begin or stop/end symbol in a flowchart is also called the ___________ symbol.
questions.explanation: The terminator symbol shows the start and end points of the flowchart (START / STOP). The process symbol shows an action, the decision symbol answers yes/no questions, and the data symbol shows input/output.

questions.stem: The ___________ symbol is used when questions such as yes or no and true or false need an answer.
questions.explanation: The decision or control symbol handles yes/no and true/false questions; the answer determines the path the algorithm flow will take.

questions.stem: The ___________ symbol is used in complex flowcharts to connect independent elements across a single page.
questions.explanation: On-page connector = SINGLE page ('A' jumps to 'A' on the same page). The near-miss trap: the link/off-page connector does the same job across MULTIPLE pages.

questions.stem: The ___________ symbol is used to show a complex process or a well-known operation.
questions.explanation: The predefined process (also called declaration) symbol shows a complex process or a well-known operation. Other symbols: database shows where data is stored; summing junction shows addition of inputs from various paths.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a principle for drawing flowcharts?
options: The flowchart should have a start point and a stop point
Flow lines should always cross each other as much as possible
Instructions for comparisons should be made as complicated as possible
The flowchart should be difficult to follow
questions.explanation: Flowchart principles: it should have a start and stop point; flow lines should generally NOT cross; comparison instructions should be as SIMPLE as possible; it should be easy to follow, neat and clear.

questions.stem: The textual representation of an algorithm is known as a ___________
questions.explanation: A pseudocode is the textual representation of the sequence of operations in a computer program (the textual representation of an algorithm). 'Textual Syntax' is a made-up distractor; a flowchart is the graphical representation.

questions.stem: _________ can be written in any notation or language while _________ are written in a combination of natural and programming language elements.
questions.explanation: Algorithms can be written in any notation or language (natural language, programming code, mathematical symbols), while pseudocodes specifically combine natural and programming language elements without strictly following any programming language's syntax.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a rule for writing pseudocode?
options: Each line in a pseudocode should only contain one statement
Keywords should be written in lowercase letters to blend with other words
Pseudocode statements should be specific to a particular programming language
Pseudocode must be written with a special software
questions.explanation: Pseudocode rules: one statement per line; keywords in CAPITAL letters; statements should be language INDEPENDENT (not tied to a language); no special software needed — any text editor works.

questions.stem: With the ___________ keyword, one or more statements are executed up to a desired number of times, based on setting some condition at the beginning/top of the statements.
questions.explanation: WHILE sets its condition at the beginning/top (WHILE condition → sequence → ENDWHILE). REPEAT-UNTIL is the near-miss: same looping purpose but the condition is set at the ending/bottom.

questions.stem: The ___________ keyword executes one or more statements based on a condition set at the ending/bottom of the statements.
questions.explanation: REPEAT-UNTIL sets the condition at the BOTTOM (REPEAT → sequence → condition). WHILE is the trap — it sets its condition at the TOP; FOR uses iteration bounds; IF-THEN-ELSE is conditional, not looping.

questions.stem: The ___________ keyword uses conditional statements to change the normal flow of operation of an algorithm.
questions.explanation: IF-THEN-ELSE changes the normal flow using conditions (IF condition THEN sequence 1 ELSE sequence 2 ENDIF). CASE does something similar but in a more generalised form.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of pseudocode?
options: There are no generally accepted standards for writing pseudocodes
Pseudocodes can be written with any text editor
Structured concepts can easily be implemented with a pseudocode
Anyone can understand pseudocode since the language is close to English
questions.explanation: Because there are no accepted standards, anyone can write pseudocode their own way, leading to various styles and possible complications. The other three options are ADVANTAGES of pseudocode — the classic flip.

questions.stem: In the pseudocode statement 'CALL AvgAge with studentAges', which keyword is used to define class objects and call functions?
questions.explanation: The CALL keyword performs operations such as defining class objects and calling functions — e.g. CALL AvgAge with studentAges, or CALL getBalance RETURNING aBalance.

questions.stem: An instance of a class is known as a ___________
questions.explanation: A class is the template (e.g. class Dog with variables + methods); objects are independently created from it — each object is an INSTANCE with its own variables and methods.

questions.stem: Because objects are not dependent on each other, each object can be independently created and maintained, and a faulty object can be removed and replaced without creating problems for the rest of the code. Which concept does this describe?
questions.explanation: Per the MIVA quiz answer key, the independence-of-objects concept is ENCAPSULATION: objects hold their own state (in variables) accessible only through their own methods, making them independent, replaceable units.

questions.stem: In programming, the state of an object is stored in ___________ and the behaviour of objects is described by ___________.
questions.explanation: Every object is defined by its state and behaviour: the state is stored in variables and the behaviour is described by methods. Only the methods of a particular object have access to that object's variables/state.

questions.stem: Real-world objects have two main characteristics; they have ___________
questions.explanation: Using the dog example: STATE = name, colour, breed, hungry; BEHAVIOUR = barking, fetching, wagging tail. Program objects mirror this: state in variables, behaviour in methods.

questions.stem: A union in 'C' is similar to a structure except that ___________
options: all of its members start at the same location in memory
it can only group items of possibly different types into a single type
it cannot have its values accessed or modified
it must always contain methods in addition to variables
questions.explanation: Struct and union both group items of possibly different types into a single type, but in a union ALL members start at the same memory location — so a union variable can represent the value of only ONE of its members at a time.

questions.stem: In C, the ___________ keyword is used to define a structure, and its members are accessed or modified using the dot syntax (.).
questions.explanation: The struct keyword defines a structure (a user-defined data type grouping items of possibly different types); its members are accessed with the dot (.). The union keyword defines a union — the near-miss distractor.

questions.stem: Classes are similar to structures but, in addition to having variables, classes also usually have ___________
questions.explanation: A class usually consists of variables such as name, breed and colour, PLUS methods such as a method that returns the name of a dog — variables + methods distinguishes classes from plain structures.

questions.stem: The fact that the state of an object can only be accessed by the object's own methods allows us to control the amount of information we share about our objects to the outside world. This is called ___________
questions.explanation: Because only an object's methods can access its state, we get information hiding — controlling how much information about the object is shared with the outside world.

questions.stem: Abstraction is the process of ___________ the internal details of an application from the outer world.
questions.explanation: Abstraction hides the internal details of an application from the outer world — like turning a car ignition without bothering about what happens inside the engine before the car starts.

questions.stem: When you twist the car key to the ignition point, you do not bother yourself with what happens in the engine between that moment and when the car actually starts. This real-world behaviour is an example of ___________
questions.explanation: The car ignition is the slides' real-world analogy for abstraction: the internal details (engine workings) are hidden from the user, who only interacts with the ignition.

questions.stem: When a programme is written such that the data of an object is not directly exposed to the outside world, and no other programme can alter the object data without obtaining the necessary permissions, ___________ has been implemented.
questions.explanation: Data abstraction = the object's DATA is not directly exposed and cannot be altered without permission. Functional abstraction = the IMPLEMENTATION of the object's METHODS is not exposed (users need only the method's name, input format and output format).

questions.stem: _________ involves writing a programme such that the implementation of the methods of an object is not directly exposed; other programmes only need to know the method's name, the format of the input, and the format of the output.
questions.explanation: Functional abstraction hides method IMPLEMENTATIONS — other programmes just need the method's name, input format and output format. Data abstraction (near-miss) hides the object's DATA instead.

questions.stem: Abstraction can be implemented by using access specifiers such as ___________ for the properties and functions of an object.
questions.explanation: The public and private access specifiers restrict the access of other programmes to only some of the properties and functions of an object — this is how abstraction is implemented in code.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit of abstraction?
options: It ensures that we can change the implementation of a method without breaking other parts of the code
It exposes the internal implementation of processes to the outside world
It prevents the reuse of code across applications
It makes applications less secure since the implementation is exposed
questions.explanation: Benefits of abstraction: more secure (implementation NOT exposed), enhanced code readability and reusability, implementation can change without breaking other parts, and no code duplication. The other options state the exact opposites.

questions.stem: By including a ___________ file as part of our code, we can easily use functions from the header file without having any knowledge of how the functions are implemented in it.
questions.explanation: Abstraction can be implemented with header files: they contain the information necessary to use libraries (such as function declarations), letting us use the functions without knowing their implementation.

questions.stem: In C, all programmes have ___________ as the entry-point function.
questions.explanation: All C programmes have main() as the entry-point function; the braces { and } describe the start and end of the function block, and printf() prints a character string to standard output.

questions.stem:
What does the following code do?

from special_functions import calculate_average
options: Imports the calculate_average function from the special_functions module
Imports the special_functions module from the calculate_average function
Imports the calculate_average module from the special_functions function
Imports the special_functions function from the calculate_average module
questions.explanation: The syntax is 'from [module] import [function]': 'from special_functions import calculate_average' imports the calculate_average FUNCTION from the special_functions MODULE. The other three options all swap the roles of module and function.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about the content of a module?
options: It contains only functions and variables
It contains only classes and objects
It contains only loops and conditions
It contains only comments and headers
questions.explanation: Per the MIVA quiz answer key, a module contains ONLY functions and variables. (Note: the lecture deck mentions modules can contain functions and classes — where the quiz key conflicts with the slides, the quiz key wins.)

questions.stem: A ___________ is a group of statements that perform a task.
questions.explanation: A function is a group of statements that perform a task. Programme codes can be separated into functions — logically the division is such that each function performs a specific task, letting different people work on smaller functions at the same time.

questions.stem: A function ___________ tells the compiler about a function name, return type, and parameters.
questions.explanation: The declaration tells the compiler the function name, return type and parameters; the actual body of the function can be defined separately (the definition).

questions.stem: A function definition consists of a function ___________ and a function ___________.
questions.explanation: A function definition provides the actual body and consists of a header and a body. The parts: return type (data type of the returned value, can be void), function name, parameters (placeholders receiving passed values), and the body (statements defining what the function does).

questions.stem: A parameter is like a ___________ ; when a function is invoked, a value is passed to the parameter.
questions.explanation: A parameter is like a placeholder: when a function is invoked, a value is passed to it. A function may contain no parameters at all.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit of using functions?
options: Functions allow us to avoid duplicating codes, because regardless of how many times a function is used, we only need to implement it once
Functions increase the amount of duplicated code in a project
Functions make it impossible to scale up a project
Functions must be rewritten each time they are needed
questions.explanation: Benefits: avoid code duplication (implement once, use many times) and easy scaling (add more functions as the project becomes complex while the system remains stable). The other options state the exact opposites.

questions.stem: Modules and functions are very similar. The main difference is that ___________
options: modules are used on a much larger scale and can contain various functions and classes
modules are used on a much smaller scale than functions
functions can contain modules, but modules cannot contain functions
functions are only used in very large projects
questions.explanation: The slides: functions solve specific problems on a smaller scale, while modules are used on a much larger scale because they can contain various functions and classes. The other options reverse or invent the relationship.

questions.stem: Which part of a recursive function stops the recursion?
questions.explanation: The base case handles the situations that are not handled properly by the recursive portion — it terminates the recursion (e.g. when counting occurrences of 42 in an array, the base case is when n = 0).

questions.stem: A function is described as recursive because it ___________
questions.explanation: A factorial function is recursive because it contains a call to itself — the computer does more work while we do less work.

questions.stem: A factorial, written as n!, is defined as ___________
options: n! = n raised to the power of 2
questions.explanation: n! = 1 * 2 * 3 * .... * (n-2) * (n-1) * n. Option C describes a SUM (like Gauss's formula), not a product — a common trap.

questions.stem: A function that contains a call to another function which eventually calls the first function is an example of ___________ recursion.
questions.explanation: Direct recursion = an explicit call to ITSELF. Indirect recursion = a call to ANOTHER function which eventually calls the first function. The trap: both involve 'calls', but only direct recursion calls itself directly.

questions.stem: A recursive function without pending operations to be performed on return from a recursive call is known as ___________
questions.explanation: Tail recursion = no pending operations after the recursive call returns. Non-tail recursion (near-miss) = there ARE pending operations to perform on return.

questions.stem: Which of the following is part of the general approach to writing recursive programs?
options: Write base case(s) to handle any situations that are not handled properly by the recursive portion
Avoid writing any base case so the recursion never stops
Replace all recursive calls with loop statements
Store every intermediate result in a global variable
questions.explanation: The general approach: write the function header, decompose into subproblems, write recursive calls to solve them, write code to combine/modify the results, and write BASE CASE(s) for everything the recursive portion cannot handle.

questions.stem: To successfully use recursion to solve a problem, we must be able to break the problem down into subproblems that are ___________ in form to the original problem.
questions.explanation: Recursive subproblems must be SIMILAR in form to the original problem (e.g. count 42s in the first n-1 elements + count 42s in the n-th element, or split the array into two halves and count in each).

questions.stem: Compared with the iterative factorial function, the recursive factorial function ___________
options: has no local variables and calculates and returns its result as a single expression
has two local variables like the iterative version
must save the solution in an intermediate variable before it can be returned
uses three statements, mirroring the iterative structure
questions.explanation: Iterative factorial: two local variables, three statements, saves the solution in an intermediate variable. Recursive factorial: NO local variables, ONE statement, returns its result as a single expression — the computer does more work while we do less.

questions.stem: _________ can be explained as the process of dividing a program's functionality into independent modules, such that each independent module has everything it needs to implement only a part of the program's functionality.
questions.explanation: Modularisation divides a program's functionality into independent modules. Decomposition is embedded in its definition: separating code into different modules and functions = decomposing the application into modules.

questions.stem: _________ describes the extent to which the functions in a module work together to achieve the ultimate aim of the module.
questions.explanation: Cohesion is about functions WITHIN a module working together — we want HIGH cohesion. Coupling (the classic near-miss) is about dependencies BETWEEN modules.

questions.stem: _________ describes the extent to which modules depend on other modules before performing their function.
questions.explanation: Coupling = dependencies BETWEEN modules; since we want modules to be independent, we usually want LOW coupling. Cohesion is the trap — it concerns functions within one module.

questions.stem: Since we want our modules to be independent, we usually want ___________
questions.explanation: High cohesion (functions in a module work together toward the module's aim) + low coupling (modules barely depend on each other) = independent modules. The single responsibility principle backs this: modules should not depend on other modules.

questions.stem: Modules should be designed so that the data structures and processing details of one module are not accessible to other modules, passing only the information required to accomplish the software functions. This hiding of unnecessary details is referred to as ___________
questions.explanation: Information hiding: modules expose only what is required through controlled interfaces. Benefits: emphasises communication through controlled interfaces, decreases the probability of adverse effects, and restricts the effects of changes in one component on others.

questions.stem: _________ is a process of modifying a software system to improve the internal structure of design without changing its external behaviour.
questions.explanation: Refactoring reduces the complexity of module design while keeping behaviour unchanged — e.g. splitting a low-cohesion component (four loosely related functions) into four high-cohesion components for easier integration, testing and maintenance.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a disadvantage of modularisation?
options: It allows large programs to be written by several or different people
Smaller modules and functions are easier and faster to design, develop, test and publish
It is easier to manage and add smaller modules and functions to our program
questions.explanation: Disadvantages: longer execution time, increased storage size, longer compilation/loading time, inter-module communication problems, and more initial design time. The other three options are ADVANTAGES — the classic flip.

questions.stem: In ___________ partitioning, the modules at the top level (control modules) perform decision-making and do little processing, whereas the modules at the low level (worker modules) perform all input, computation and output tasks.
questions.explanation: Vertical partitioning distributes functionality top-down: control modules decide, worker modules do the work. Horizontal partitioning (near-miss) uses control modules to communicate between functions and requires passing more data across module interfaces.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a functional testing method?
questions.explanation: Functional testing methods = unit, integration, acceptance and system testing. Usability testing belongs to NON-functional methods (usability, performance, security, compatibility) — the odd one out.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a non-functional testing method?
questions.explanation: Non-functional methods = usability, performance, security and compatibility. System testing is FUNCTIONAL — it tests the system as a whole after integration to confirm technical and functional requirements are met.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a software testing life cycle phase?
questions.explanation: STLC phases run from requirement analysis to test cycle closure (requirement analysis, planning, test case development, environment setup, execution, closure). 'Software design and development' is BUILDING the software (SDLC) — it happens outside the testing life cycle.

questions.stem: Which software testing approach focuses on testing independent units or components to identify bugs or errors?
questions.explanation: Unit testing checks execution paths of independent units — unit tests are mostly carried out on the FUNCTIONS in the program, one unit at a time. Integration tests how parts work TOGETHER; system tests the whole; acceptance confirms requirements.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a widely used debugger for identifying and resolving bugs?
questions.explanation: WinDbg (Windows debugger), Radare2 (reverse-engineering/debugging framework) and Valgrind (memory debugging toolset) are all real debugging tools. Photoshop is IMAGE EDITING software — a cross-domain fake.

questions.stem: Why is the test environment setup phase important in the software testing life cycle?
options: It defines the roles and responsibilities of the testing team
It determines the overall project schedule
It establishes a controlled and stable environment for testing activities
It ensures the accuracy of test case execution
questions.explanation: Test environment setup provisions the hardware/software/tools/configuration where tests run — a controlled, stable space so results are not skewed by environmental issues. Roles, schedule and resources belong to the TEST PLANNING phase.
questions.mivaHints: Slide 6, Software Testing Life Cycle and Debugging

questions.stem: In the ___________ phase, the testing strategy, cost, and duration are clearly defined.
questions.explanation: The test plan identifies the SCOPE of testing, the TYPES of tests to be performed and the RESOURCES needed — strategy, cost and duration are planning decisions. Requirement analysis only figures out what needs testing.

questions.stem: _________ testing methods are used to test the computer program to ensure that the program performs as expected, such as testing if an addition function works as expected.
questions.explanation: Functional testing checks that the program performs as expected (unit, integration, acceptance, system). Non-functional testing checks aspects like the user interface, security, performance and compatibility.

questions.stem: _________ tests are used to test how well different parts of a software work together, and can either be top-down or bottom-up.
questions.explanation: Integration tests check how different parts work TOGETHER: top-down tests higher-level modules first; bottom-up tests lower-level modules first. Unit testing (the trap) tests independent units — not combinations.

questions.stem: _________ tests are used to test the system as a whole after all the parts are integrated, to confirm that the software meets the technical and functional requirements.
questions.explanation: System testing = the system AS A WHOLE after integration, confirming technical and functional requirements. Acceptance tests confirm the software meets EXPECTED requirements and catch bugs causing major errors and crashes.
